budget._source: design/03 Appendix B rows 4-5 and §1.1; design/08 §5. CI fails the build on breach (R9). Loosening any line here is a reviewed change to this file with the reason in the commit message.

_gatedBy.bench:compile: every PR — the compile, structure and decode sections. Deterministic, no database.
_gatedBy.bench:runtime: nightly on the fixed runner, and on a PR labelled `perf` — adds the nine end-to-end pairs.

_design._why: design/03 §1.1 and design/08 §5's own numbers, printed beside the measurement so drift from the design document is visible even inside budget (R9).

compile._why: Two kinds of line. `emitP50Us` is design/03 §1.1's own number, gated absolutely because the emitter measures ~4.4 us against it -- ~5.7x headroom, which no runner can flake. Everything tighter is a RATIO to sampler.mjs's fixed reference workload measured in the same process, for the reason design/08 §5 gives for the DB cases: a wall-clock budget loose enough not to flake on a shared runner is too loose to notice a 30% regression. The bytes/op lines are the tight ones, because allocation is machine-INDEPENDENT (+/-0.2% across runs here) and design/08 §5 names it as where ORM overhead hides. Headroom was sized by running this bench 3x idle and 3x while `pnpm test:live` saturated the machine; design/09 §3.7 records both spreads.
compile._whySimpleSelectsPerSecond: design/08 §5 asks for 200 000/s and the builder-plus-compile path measures 97k-142k on the reference machine (design/09 §3.7 finding 2). The floor here is the measured behaviour with headroom, not the design number, and the three-way print carries the 200 000 next to it on every run so the gap cannot be forgotten. Closing it means reducing the 39 KB a compile allocates, which is builder work and is booked as a deferral, not a budget edit.
compile._whyBuildAndCompileRefRatioIsCoarse: Measured 8.4-11.7 idle and 21.6 while `pnpm test:live` saturated the machine, with bytes/op moving 0.2% across the same six runs. The reference workload tracks CPU speed well and memory/GC pressure only roughly, and this path allocates 39 KB per call -- so its wall clock is the one number here that a busy machine really can move. The budget is therefore a CATASTROPHE guard, not a regression detector; the regression detector for this path is `buildAndCompileBytes`. design/08 §5 makes this argument about shared CI runners; measuring it made the same argument one level further in.

decode._why: design/03 Appendix B says 'within 15% of a hand-written positional mapper' and does not say what the mapper may skip. Measured (design/09 §3.7), that is the whole question, so three pairs are gated instead of one. None sits at 1.15 and none is meant to: the numbers below are the measured behaviour plus headroom, and the design number is printed beside every one of them so the gap stays visible (R9). Bringing any of them to 1.15 needs `new Function` codegen for the row loop, which src/compile/decode.ts rules out by default on CSP grounds and offers as an opt-in flag exactly when 'benchmarks later disagree' -- they now do, and design/09 §3.7 books it as a named deferral rather than widening this file again.
decode._notGated: `decode · row-loop dispatch only` is reported, never gated. It pairs a decoder built over twelve `text` (identity) codecs against a literal-object copy, so the denominator is ~70 us for 10 000 rows and the ratio swings 21-47 with the sample size and the machine. It is a decomposition -- it says the closure tree's row loop is ~20-30x a literal object and that this is ~20% of a real decode -- not an Appendix B row, and a gate on it would be a gate on noise.

e2e._why: design/08 §5's gate is p50 <= 1.15x and p99 <= 1.30x raw `pg`, on all nine cases. Measured on PostgreSQL 17.11 (design/09 §3.7), five of the nine sit between 1.17 and 1.36 at p50 and one -- the 1 000-row batch insert -- at 1.79, so a single 1.15 line would be red on the day it was written. The budgets are therefore PER CASE and measured, with the design number printed beside every one of them on every run so the gap cannot be forgotten. The shape of the gap is the useful part and it is booked in §3.7: our overhead is a roughly constant ~0.05-0.19 ms of client-side work per statement, which is ~20-35% of a point select and ~1% of a relation load, plus real encoding work in the batch insert.
e2e._whyP99IsLoose: design/08 §5 gates p99 <= 1.30x and the gate is kept, but it is kept HONEST rather than tight. Across five runs on the reference machine the p50 ratios reproduced to +/-0.1 and the p95 ratios to about +/-0.4, while the SAME p99 line moved 0.44 -> 10.92 for `delete by PK` and 0.79 -> 4.38 for the batch insert: a 99th percentile over 40-100 samples of a sub-millisecond round trip is one scheduler stall wide, and no sample count this harness can afford fixes that on a machine it does not own. So p99 is a uniform 12x catastrophe guard and `overheadP95` is the tail gate that actually holds. Tightening p99 wants the fixed nightly runner's numbers, which is one nightly run away; design/09 §3.7 records that as unverified rather than guessing.
e2e._whyP95Exists: A deviation from design/08 §5, which names p50 and p99 only. p95 was added because it is the tightest tail statistic this harness measures reproducibly: across six runs on the reference machine p50 moved +/-0.1 and p95 +/-0.4, while the same p99 line moved 0.44 -> 10.92. The p95 budgets are ~1.6x the WORST of those six runs -- a tail guard, not a tight bound, because even p95 shows the occasional excursion (the 1 000-row select read 1.13-1.22 five times and 1.96 once). Tightening them wants the fixed nightly runner's distribution; guessing one from a laptop and calling it a gate is what R9 exists to stop. The p99 line stays so design/08 §5's number keeps its place in the print.

_caveats: The `…RefRatio` gates divide by sampler.mjs's reference workload. It tracks CPU speed well and GC pressure only roughly, so the build-and-compile ratio is the noisiest line here (8.4-11.7 across six runs on one machine); the tight gate on that path is bytes/op, not time.
`decode · row-loop dispatch only` is reported, not gated -- see decode._notGated.

_designLinked._why: Which gated line corresponds to which design number, so that widening a budget past its design number is a MACHINE-checkable event and not only a review one (R9). `run.mjs` fails when a linked budget exceeds its design value unless the metric is named in `_overDesign` — which is what turns 'loosening a budget is a reviewed change with a reason' from a convention into a gate.

_overDesign._why: Every entry is a budget that is deliberately looser than design's number, with the reason. Adding one is the reviewed act R9 describes; the three-way print keeps the design number visible next to the measurement for as long as the entry exists.
_overDesign.compile.simpleSelectsPerSecond: design/08 §5 asks 200 000/s of the builder-chain-plus-compile path; measured 92k-142k on the reference machine. The gap is 39 KB of allocation per compile (design/09 §3.7 finding 2), which is builder work and is booked as a deferral rather than paid for by editing this number again.
_overDesign.decode.ratioVsUncheckedMapperP50: design/03 Appendix B asks for 1.15x a hand-written positional mapper; measured 2.70-2.99. ~45% of the gap is validation the unchecked mapper skips and the rest is the closure tree's per-cell dispatch and dynamic-key row construction (design/09 §3.7 finding 1).
_overDesign.decode.ratioVsCheckedMapperP50: the same measurement against a mapper that performs the codecs' own checks: 1.55-1.65. This is the honest 'what does the closure tree cost' number and it is still above 1.15; closing it needs the codegen decode.ts rules out by default on CSP grounds.
_overDesign.e2e.overheadP50: design/08 §5 asks p50 <= 1.15x on all nine; measured 1.01-1.83 (design/09 §3.7). The overhead is a roughly constant ~0.03-0.15 ms of client-side work per statement plus real codec encoding in the batch insert, so it is ~1% of a relation load and ~1.8x of a 1 000-row batch. Per-case budgets, each measured.
_overDesign.e2e.overheadP95: the tail gate design/08 §5 does not name; see e2e._whyP95Exists.
_overDesign.e2e.overheadP99: a uniform 12x catastrophe guard; see e2e._whyP99IsLoose.
